## Unpacking diversity: How to read a evolutionary tree
<hr>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:220px; LEFT:550px; WIDTH:550px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/phylo.png">


- **Depicts evolutionary relationships amongst selected taxa**
    - hypothetical
    - taxon (singular) can be species or group

<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 55%;">

- **Taxa at ends of tree are usually living (extant)**
    - taxa not at the end are extinct
    
<br/>

- **Taxa are connected by branches, which join at nodes**
    - node represents ancestor shared by 2+ taxa
    - branch length may or may not mean something
    
<br/>

- **Infer degree of relationship based on nodes**
    - 2 human virus are more closely related to one another that either is to bat virus.

</div>

## Nodes in cladograms represent divergences or speciation events
<hr>

**Each node indicates the common ancestors of descendants**

<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>

**Unique history (divergence or speciation) represents key genetic change**

<br/>

**Sometimes represented as morphological (structural) trait in a phylogeny**

## Evolution keep rolling, so species are not fixed in a hierarchy
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:25px; WIDTH:500px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/bird.png">


<div style="float: right; width: 50%;">

- **Species do change (within populations), species go extinct, new species arise**

<br/>

- **Appalachian Mountain Examples:**
    + rainbow and brook trout populations in Linville caves (NC) are blind
    + Eastern elk and Eastern bison are extinct
    + Appalachian tiger swallowtail butterfly evolved from interbreeding of the Eastern and Canadian tiger swallowtail species (a successfull hybrid!)
    
</div>

## Change occurs across all biological scales
<hr>

- **Genes - Organisms - Populations - Species - Communities - Ecosystems - Biosphere**

<br/>

- **All are interconnected and thus all are influenced by environmental change**

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:300px; LEFT:100px; WIDTH:400px; HEIGHT:350px" SRC="images/mutationrate.png">

## Mountains (e.g., Appalachia) and changing climates
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>

<div style="float: right; width: 50%;">

- **Since animals are adapted to a range of climate, what happens on mountains?**

<br/>

- **Climate change is likely to reduce the range size of amphibians and mammals in Appalachian forests**
    + will endemic species go extinct?

<br/>

- **Birds and reptiles are more likely to expand their range size under long-term climate scenarios in Appalachian forests**
    + which species will they replace?

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:220px; LEFT:0px; WIDTH:500px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/mountain.jpg">

## Change occurs at molecular level
<hr>

- **Once there is variation, there are two main processes that can work on that variation and lead to long term evolution**
    - <span style="color:blue">*Natural Selection*</span>
    - <span style="color:blue">*Genetic Drift*</span>


<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:290px; LEFT:50px; WIDTH:1000px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/survival.png">

## Genetic drift (non-adaptive evolution)
<hr>
**More gametes (sperm and egg) are produced than seed the next generation**

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:240px; LEFT:50px; WIDTH:1000px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/gametes.png">


## Genetic drift
<hr>
**Random sampling gametes can change the genetic composition of a population over time**

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:220px; LEFT:250px; WIDTH:600px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/gametes2.png">

## Genetic drift can have rapid effects during a “bottleneck"
<hr>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:180px; LEFT:100px; WIDTH:900px; HEIGHT:500px" SRC="images/bottle.png">

## Genetic drift in the wild
<hr>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:160px; LEFT:150px; WIDTH:800px; HEIGHT:500px" SRC="images/bison.png">


## Selection and Drift
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>

- **Selection and drift are both always happening simultaneously**
    - drift is by chance alone
    - selection is by reproductive success
    
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>

- **But they are not always equally strong**

<br/>

- **Both processes can lead not only to change within populations but also divergence between populations**

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:250px; LEFT:580px; WIDTH:340px; HEIGHT:200px" SRC="images/versus.jpg">
